disease_name: Postpartum hemorrhage due to uterine atony / 弛緩出血

distillation_scope.disease_name_only_prompt: Postpartum hemorrhage due to uterine atony
distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer postpartum hemorrhage leaf for failure of postpartum myometrial contraction and placental-bed compression. Retained placenta, genital tract trauma, uterine rupture, placenta accreta spectrum, uterine inversion, amniotic fluid embolism, placental abruption, and primary coagulopathy are represented as context, mimic, source-control, or vector-superposition axes rather than disease-name qualifiers.
distillation_scope.boundary_policy: This manifold explains postpartum bleeding through inadequate uterine tone after delivery. If bleeding is mainly from retained tissue, laceration, rupture, inversion, DIC, AFE, or abruption, those facts should enter as separate axes or competing/superposed manifolds and should not be double-counted as atony on the same axes.
distillation_scope.ranking_note: Presentation ranking may consume postpartum timing, completed delivery, boggy enlarged uterus, reduced fundal tone, heavy vaginal/postpartum bleeding, quantified blood loss, response to massage/uterotonics, tachycardia, hypotension, hemoglobin fall, lactate, urine output, transfusion need, and absence or presence of retained placenta, laceration, rupture, inversion, or severe coagulopathy as structured context.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Uterine atony is the defining pathophysiology of this leaf, so the core myometrial contraction-failure activity should be high when the atony manifold is active.
Persistent placental-bed bleeding is the direct bleeding geometry of atonic postpartum hemorrhage.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Uterine overdistension or myometrial exhaustion context
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Multiple gestation, polyhydramnios, macrosomia, prolonged labor, high-dose oxytocin exposure, chorioamnionitis, grand multiparity, or operative delivery can reduce effective postpartum tone and increase atony risk.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Oxytocin signaling desensitization or uterine relaxation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Prolonged exposure to oxytocin, magnesium sulfate, volatile anesthetics, tocolytics, infection, or metabolic stress can blunt calcium-mediated myometrial contraction.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Hemorrhagic volume loss and oxygen-delivery failure
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Blood-loss physiology ranges from compensated hemorrhage to profound shock in uterine-atony postpartum hemorrhage.

Large-volume hemorrhage, crystalloid, delayed blood products, hypothermia, acidosis, obstetric tissue-factor disease, or baseline anticoagulation can impair clot stability and amplify bleeding. This is an amplifier or superposition context, not the initiating atony identity.

Bimanual compression, uterine massage, oxytocin, prostaglandins, ergot alkaloids, tamponade, or surgical compression can restore placental-bed compression and lower bleeding if atony remains the main source.

Bleeding persists despite tone-directed therapy when atony is severe, treatment is delayed, uterine tissue is nonresponsive, blood products are unavailable, or another source such as retained tissue, trauma, rupture, accreta, or DIC is active.

Overdistended or exhausted myometrium contracts poorly after delivery.
Receptor desensitization or uterine relaxation lowers postpartum tone.
Weak myometrial contraction fails to clamp uteroplacental vessels.
Ongoing uterine bleeding rapidly depletes intravascular volume.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Stronger with delayed balanced transfusion, hypothermia, acidosis, massive bleeding, or obstetric DIC superposition.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Hemorrhage and resuscitation can produce or reveal coagulopathy that further destabilizes hemostasis.

Tone-directed therapy restores myometrial contraction when atony is active.
Improved uterine tone compresses placental-bed vessels and lowers bleeding rate.

supportive_care: Timestamp delivery, placental delivery, onset of bleeding, uterine tone findings, quantified blood loss, vital signs, uterotonic dosing, transfusion, procedures, and response.

Keep Tone, Tissue, Trauma, and Thrombin causes distinct: atony explains soft/boggy uterus and tone-responsive bleeding; retained placenta, laceration, rupture, inversion, accreta, and coagulopathy remain structured context or competing/superposed manifolds.

Do not delete bleeding evidence when the uterus is firm; instead raise genital_tract_laceration_presence, uterine_rupture_context_presence, source_control_need, or coagulopathy axes as medically true.
Assess uterine tone and fundal height repeatedly after massage and uterotonics because recurrent atony can follow transient response.

Quantify cumulative blood loss rather than relying only on subjective visual severity; trend hemoglobin, lactate, urine output, MAP, fibrinogen, platelets, PT/INR, aPTT, temperature, calcium, and acid-base status during active hemorrhage.
Activate obstetric hemorrhage, anesthesia, blood bank, operating-room, interventional radiology, and ICU pathways early when bleeding, shock, coagulopathy, or source-control need is high.
Model overt DIC, AFE, abruption, uterine rupture, or transfusion reaction as additional disease/event geometry when present; do not let this atony leaf double-count their disease-specific axes.

Treatment choice should emerge from uterine tone, bleeding rate, retained tissue, trauma/rupture context, coagulopathy, shock, contraindication axes, blood-product availability, and local procedural access.
